The journey ended in Osaka. After 650 kilometers of walking from Tokyo—guitar strapped to his back, soles of his boots worn thin—a young Dutch traveler finally met his friends.

He had kept the trek a secret until the moment he arrived. When he revealed that he hadn't taken the Shinkansen, but had instead traced the long, historical Tokaido path on foot, his friends reacted with a mix of shock and envy.

One friend captured their sentiment:

> *"Holland guys... they always do stuff like that!"*

In that moment, the walk wasn't just a personal feat; it was archetypal. It was "The Dutch Way"—a blend of quiet ruggedness, a touch of madness, and a total lack of fanfare.

---

10 years, I combined a visit to my sister and her husband who was working in Toulouse with a business trip to Venlo, Netherlands.

I let my contact, Pieter know that I am in France.

He suggested that I take a long-range trains to Netherlands via overnight trains through Paris, Antewerp and Rotterdam.

A distance of nearly 1200km and taking 15 hours of travel time.

This was based on our previous discussions

He would go over his honeymoon trip to Switzerland on a train. A 800km journey and 12 hours.

I would tell him about the 600km journey from Singapore's Tanjong Pagar Station to Wakauf Bahru Station in Kelantan region of eastern Malaysia peninsula.

I held ace on this discussion

The longest journey on a train for me was the Tokyo to Sapporo. A 1200km trip that took 16 hours before Shinkansen implementation.

Flying from point A to point B was not of interest to either one of us.

---

When I worked in Gumi, Korea, the company canteen provided 3 meals a day

Meals were finished in matter of minutes and most people either smoked, drank coffee or played 족구.

Though I haven't had Korean military training, I imagined the company ran like a military garrison.

Everyone understood their roles, don't step outside its bounds and keep working at the task at hand.

And prevailing mode was 빨리빠리.

Get things done and move on to the next project.

I catch myself thinking in that mode from time to time. Wanting to belong to an established group, a safe approach.

But I also see the meaning and depth in the Dutch-Approach.

Take things slow, see things for yourself, establish your own set of rules on how things are and the way it should be.

My current thinking is that the meal and the discussion is just as important as the activity that follows or replaces it.

When it comes to travel, the slower is better. Especially if one can carry one's own burden and see and interact with nature as did Eddie van der Meer.

Keeping our journeys and travel secret since the benefit is personal, whether it is made public or not.
